ox: Incorrect. Degradation would give several smaller bands on SDS-PAGE, not one clean 50 kDa band, and a degraded protein would elute LATER (smaller), not earlier.
Incorrect. SDS does not add 150 kDa of mass. It coats the protein with negative charge in proportion to its length, so all proteins run by size alone.

Correct. SDS-PAGE breaks the complex apart and reports ONE subunit (50 kDa). Gel filtration keeps the native complex together and reports its whole size (200 kDa). 200 ÷ 50 = 4, so it is a tetramer of identical subunits.
Incorrect. A monomer with disulfide bonds would still weigh 50 kDa in the native state and would elute near 50 kDa, not 200 kDa.

p: SDS-PAGE uses a detergent that unfolds the protein and gives it a uniform negative charge, so it separates by chain mass and reports ONE subunit. Gel filtration (size exclusion) separates native, folded complexes by size and reports the whole assembly. Dividing the native size by the subunit size gives the number of subunits.

x5C_063.trap: Believing SDS adds mass; it only adds charge in proportion to length.
mem: SDS-PAGE separates by mass only (SDS denatures and coats with uniform negative charge).
Gel filtration: bigger complexes elute FIRST, smaller ones later.
Native size ÷ SDS-PAGE size = number of identical subunits.

fm.f: number of subunits = native size ÷ subunit size, where native size = whole complex from gel filtration, subunit size = one chain from SDS-PAGE
fm.why: We divide because the complex is made of identical pieces whose masses add up.

x5C_063.sc: Divide the big number by the small number: 200 ÷ 50 = 4.
x5C_063.plain: SDS-PAGE takes a LEGO castle apart and weighs one brick. Gel filtration weighs the whole castle.

ox: Incorrect. SDS does not break peptide bonds under any conditions. Peptide bonds are broken only by hydrolysis (acid or proteases).
Incorrect. SDS disrupts noncovalent forces. If only noncovalent forces held the chains, the 150 kDa band would have split even WITHOUT the reducing agent.
Incorrect. β-Mercaptoethanol reduces disulfide bonds; it does not remove sugars. Sugar removal would need a glycosidase.

Correct. The 150 kDa band survives SDS, so the chains must be held by COVALENT links. Adding β-mercaptoethanol breaks disulfides and releases the chains. Check: 2 heavy × 50 + 2 light × 25 = 100 + 50 = 150 kDa.

p: SDS unfolds proteins and disrupts noncovalent interactions, but it does not break covalent bonds such as disulfides. A reducing agent (β-mercaptoethanol or DTT) breaks disulfide bonds. If a band is bigger without the reducing agent and splits into pieces with it, the pieces were joined by disulfide bonds. An IgG antibody is two heavy and two light chains joined this way.

x5C_081.trap: Believing SDS alone separates chains held together by disulfides.
mem: Reducing agents (β-ME, DTT) break disulfide bonds.
SDS breaks noncovalent bonds but NOT covalent bonds.
IgG = 2 heavy (≈ 50 kDa) + 2 light (≈ 25 kDa) chains joined by disulfides ≈ 150 kDa.

fm.f: total mass = (number of heavy chains × heavy mass) + (number of light chains × light mass)
fm.why: We add the masses of all chains to check that the pieces really make up the whole antibody.

x5C_081.sc: Bigger band without reducing agent that splits WITH it = pieces were joined by disulfides.
x5C_081.plain: β-Mercaptoethanol is scissors for the staples (disulfide bonds) that hold the chains together; SDS alone cannot cut staples.

ox: Wrong. DNA does not go to the cathode, and larger fragments move slower, so both parts are wrong.
Wrong. The direction (anode) is right, but larger fragments move slower, not faster. Big pieces get stuck in the gel pores.
Correct. DNA's phosphate backbone is negative, so it moves toward the positive anode. Smaller fragments wiggle through the gel pores faster, so they travel farther.
Wrong. Negative DNA is repelled by the negative cathode, so the direction is wrong. The size part is right.

p: Electrophoresis uses an electric field to move charged molecules through a gel. DNA has a negative charge from its phosphate backbone, so it runs toward the positive electrode (anode).
The gel is a mesh of tiny pores. Small fragments slip through quickly, large ones get slowed down. After a run, small pieces sit near the far end.

mem: DNA is negative, so it moves to the anode (+).
Smaller fragments travel farther.
Charge-to-mass is the same for all DNA, so size decides speed.
d_5C_21.mn: Opposites attract: negative DNA runs to the positive pole.
d_5C_21.trap: Forgetting DNA is negative, or reversing which size moves faster.
d_5C_21.plain: Like running through a thick forest. A small kid darts between trees fast, but a kid carrying a big sheet gets stuck.

ox: Wrong. Two liquids with close boiling points need fractional distillation, not sublimation.
Correct. A solid with significant vapor pressure below its melting point turns straight to gas, then re-deposits on a cold surface as pure crystals. Nonvolatile impurities stay behind.
Wrong. A dissolved salt is recovered by evaporating the water or by crystallization. Salt does not sublime.
Wrong. Proteins differing in mass are separated by chromatography or electrophoresis. Proteins do not vaporize.

p: Sublimation is a solid turning directly into a gas without becoming liquid. Some solids, like iodine, caffeine or naphthalene, have enough vapor pressure to do this when heated gently.
Collect the gas on a cold surface and it becomes solid again, pure. Impurities that cannot vaporize stay behind.

mem: Sublimation: solid to gas directly.
Deposition: gas to solid directly.
Works if the solid is volatile and impurities are not.
d_5C_28.trap: Thinking sublimation applies only to dry ice. Many other solids can be purified this way.
d_5C_28.plain: Like frost on a cold window. Water vapor in the air skips being liquid and sticks as ice, leaving dust behind.

ox: Correct. Silica is very polar. The least polar compound sticks to it the least and is carried farthest by the nonpolar eluent, so it has the highest Rf.
Wrong. The most polar compound binds strongly to polar silica and stays near the start. The trap is thinking 'like dissolves like' for the wrong phase.
Wrong. TLC on silica separates mainly by polarity here, not by mass.
Wrong. If all traveled equally there would be no separation. Differences in polarity make them move differently.

p: TLC has a stationary phase (silica gel, which is polar) on a plate and a mobile phase (the eluent) that climbs the plate. Each compound is pulled by the silica and by the eluent.
Polar compounds stick to polar silica and move little. Nonpolar compounds move with the eluent. Rf = distance compound traveled / distance solvent traveled.

mem: Silica is polar, so polar compounds have low Rf.
Nonpolar compounds have high Rf.
A more polar eluent raises all Rf values.

fm.f: Rf = d(compound) / d(solvent), where d(compound) = distance the spot moved, d(solvent) = distance the solvent front moved
fm.v: Example only, no numbers given in the question
fm.s: Rf is between 0 and 1. A higher Rf means a less polar compound
fm.why: Rf tells how far a compound travels relative to the solvent.
fm.nc: No calculation needed here, just compare polarity.

q77.trap: Mixing up which compound sticks to silica. Polar sticks, nonpolar travels.
q77.plain: Like running through sticky mud versus a smooth floor. Greasy shoes (nonpolar) slide fast along a clean floor; shoes that stick to the mud (polar) hardly move.

ox: Correct. Carboxylic acids (pKa about 4-5) are strong enough to be deprotonated by bicarbonate. They become water-soluble carboxylate salts and move into the water layer.
Wrong. Phenols (pKa about 10) are weaker acids than carbonic acid, so bicarbonate does not deprotonate them. Stronger base such as NaOH is needed.
Wrong. Amines are bases. They are extracted into water by washing with aqueous acid (like HCl), not base.
Wrong. A neutral alcohol is not acidic enough and stays neutral, so it remains in the ether layer.

p: Extraction separates compounds by changing their charge. A charged compound dissolves in water, and a neutral one stays in the organic layer (ether).
Sodium bicarbonate is a weak base. It removes H+ only from strong enough acids like carboxylic acids, turning them into water-soluble salts. Phenols need NaOH. Amines need acid.

mem: NaHCO3 extracts carboxylic acids only.
NaOH extracts carboxylic acids and phenols.
HCl extracts amines (bases).
q78.trap: Assuming any acid is removed by bicarbonate. Phenols are too weak.
q78.plain: Giving a coat to some kids so they can join the water-park group. Bicarbonate only dresses up the acid kids that are strong enough, and the others stay behind in the ether.

ox: Correct. SDS (a detergent) coats proteins with negative charge in proportion to their length, so charge per mass is the same for all. Only size then matters, and small proteins slip through the gel pores fastest and travel farthest.
Wrong. This is the trap of thinking charge drives the separation. SDS covers the protein's own charge, so native charge no longer matters.
Wrong. Separation by isoelectric point (pI) is isoelectric focusing, a different technique that uses a pH gradient. Do not mix up the two gel methods.
Wrong. This reverses the direction. Large proteins get stuck in the gel mesh and move the shortest distance.

p: SDS-PAGE is a way to sort proteins by size. SDS is a detergent that unfolds proteins and coats them with negative charge. Every protein ends up with about the same charge per unit of length.
The proteins are pulled through a gel (a jelly-like mesh) by an electric current toward the positive end. Small proteins fit through the mesh easily and move far. Large ones are slowed.

mem: SDS-PAGE separates by mass only; SDS hides native charge and shape
Smaller proteins travel farther; larger ones stay near the top (wells)
Isoelectric focusing separates by pI, not by mass
Native PAGE keeps charge and shape, so it separates by both
q79.trap: Choosing charge or pI because gels use electricity. SDS erases charge differences, so size alone decides.
q79.plain: Think of running through a crowded hallway. A small kid weaves through quickly, while a big person with a huge backpack gets stuck.

ox: Correct. When boiling points are close (less than about 25 °C apart), one round of boiling and condensing barely separates the liquids. A fractionating column adds many repeat cycles, which gives a clean separation.
Wrong. With a gap above about 100 °C, simple distillation already works well. The trap is thinking a harder separation needs a bigger gap.
Wrong. Distillation separates liquids by boiling point. Solids are separated by methods like filtration or recrystallization.
Wrong. Enantiomers have identical physical properties, including boiling point, so no distillation can separate them. They need a chiral method.

p: Distillation separates liquids by boiling point. The mixture is heated, the vapor is richer in the more volatile liquid (the one that boils at the lower temperature), and the vapor is cooled back into liquid.
Simple distillation is one cycle. Fractional distillation adds a packed column so the vapor condenses and re-vaporizes many times. Use it when boiling points are close.

mem: Simple distillation: boiling points differ by more than about 25 to 100 °C
Fractional distillation: boiling points closer than about 25 °C
Enantiomers have the same boiling point, so distillation cannot split them
Distillation is for liquids
q80.trap: Picking the large boiling-point gap for fractional distillation. A large gap means the easy method is enough.
q80.plain: Simple distillation is sorting laundry once. Fractional distillation is sorting it again and again until every sock matches.

ox: Correct. Two liquids that do not mix stack by density. Ether is 0.71 g/mL and water is 1.00 g/mL, so the lighter ether floats on top.
Wrong. The idea that organic layers always sink is false. They sink only if denser than water, like dichloromethane. Ether is lighter.
Wrong. Polarity decides whether liquids mix, not which one is on top. Also, ether is less polar than water, so the reasoning is backward.
Wrong. Ether and water are largely immiscible, so they form two layers. They do not make one mixed phase.

p: A separatory funnel holds two liquids that do not mix (immiscible). They form two layers. The denser liquid (more mass per mL) goes to the bottom.
Density is the only thing that decides which layer is on top. Water is 1.00 g/mL. Any liquid below 1.00 floats on water. Any liquid above 1.00 sinks.

mem: Top layer = lower density
Water is 1.00 g/mL
Ether, hexane, ethyl acetate float on water
Dichloromethane and chloroform sink below water
x5C_002.trap: Assuming organic means top. Always compare the density number to 1.00.
x5C_002.plain: Oil floats on water in a salad dressing bottle. The lighter liquid always rides on top.

ox: Wrong. This assumes organic solvents always float. Dichloromethane is 1.33 g/mL, denser than water, so the organic layer is on the bottom.
Wrong. Water (1.00 g/mL) is the top layer here, and it is the aqueous phase. Keeping it would throw away the product, which moved into the organic layer.
Wrong. The product does not split evenly. A neutral organic compound strongly prefers the organic solvent, so it is mostly in one layer.
Correct. Dichloromethane (1.33) is denser than water (1.00), so the organic layer sits at the bottom. The product moved there, so drain the bottom layer through the stopcock and keep it.

p: In an extraction, the product moves into the solvent it likes best. A neutral organic product moves into the organic solvent.
Then you must find which layer that is. Compare density to water (1.00 g/mL). Denser solvents like dichloromethane sit on the bottom and are drained out first.

mem: Bottom layer = denser liquid
Dichloromethane is denser than water, so it is the bottom layer
Neutral organic products go into the organic layer
Never throw away a layer until you have found your product
x5C_003.trap: Assuming the organic layer is always on top. Check density first.
x5C_003.plain: It is like knowing which shelf holds your toy. First find which liquid is heavier, then you know which layer is at the bottom.

ox: Wrong. Bicarbonate is a weak base (its conjugate acid has pKa about 6.4). It cannot pull the proton off a phenol (pKa about 10). It removes only stronger acids like carboxylic acids.
Correct. Hydroxide is a strong base (conjugate acid water, pKa about 15.7). It removes the phenol's proton, making charged phenoxide, which dissolves in water. Naphthalene stays in the ether.
Wrong. Acid keeps the phenol protonated and neutral, so it stays in the ether. HCl would remove bases such as amines instead.
Wrong. Brine (salt water) just helps dry the organic layer. It does not react with the phenol.

p: A neutral molecule dissolves in organic solvent. A charged molecule (an ion) dissolves in water. To move an acid into water, add a base strong enough to remove its proton and make it an ion.
The base works only if its conjugate acid has a higher pKa than the acid you are removing. Phenol pKa is about 10, so you need hydroxide.

mem: Carboxylic acid pKa about 4-5: NaHCO3 works
Phenol pKa about 10: needs NaOH
Base converts an acid to a water-soluble salt
HCl pulls amines into water
x5C_004.trap: Using bicarbonate for a phenol. It is too weak. Compare the pKa values.
x5C_004.plain: It is like putting a floaty vest on someone so they leave the oil pool and move into the water pool. Only a strong enough push (base) does it.

ox: Wrong. Benzoic acid is a carboxylic acid, and the earlier NaHCO3 wash already removed it as sodium benzoate. It is not left for the NaOH wash.
Wrong. Naphthalene has no acidic hydrogen, so no base can ionize it. It stays in the ether to the end.
Correct. Bicarbonate took only benzoic acid (pKa about 4-5). 2-Naphthol (a phenol, pKa about 10) remained, and NaOH then converts it to sodium naphthoxide, which goes into water.
Wrong. Both would be in the NaOH extract only if NaOH were used first. Here the weak base went first and removed benzoate.

p: You can separate several acids by washing with bases of rising strength. A weak base takes only the strongest acid. A stronger base then takes the next acid.
Here: NaHCO3 takes the carboxylic acid. NaOH then takes the phenol. The neutral compound (naphthalene) never leaves the ether.

mem: Order: weak base first, strong base second
NaHCO3 removes carboxylic acids only
NaOH removes phenols too
Neutral compounds stay in the organic layer
x5C_008.trap: Forgetting the order. If NaOH came first, both acids would go together.
x5C_008.plain: Like a sieve with big holes first, then small holes. Each step catches one size and lets the rest pass.

ox: Wrong. One big extraction leaves more solute behind. This is the common guess that more solvent at once is best.
Wrong. Equal total volume does not mean equal recovery. Each fresh portion pulls out a fraction of what is left, so splitting helps.
Wrong. Heating a closed funnel with a volatile solvent builds pressure and is dangerous. It also does not improve partitioning.
Correct. Each fresh portion removes a fraction of the solute still in the water. Repeating this shrinks what remains faster than one large portion does.

p: Each time you add fresh solvent, the solute splits between the two layers by a fixed ratio. Fresh solvent restarts that split on whatever is left in the water.
So three small portions pull out more than one portion three times as big. The leftover shrinks by a fraction each time.

mem: Several small extractions beat one large extraction of the same total volume
Each extraction removes a fixed fraction of what remains
Recovery never reaches exactly 100%
x5C_009.trap: Thinking total solvent volume alone decides recovery. How you split it matters.
x5C_009.plain: Rinsing a muddy cup three times with a little water cleans it better than one big rinse.

ox: Wrong. 0.67 g is only the first 50 mL pass (2/3 of the solute). The question asks for both passes.
Wrong. 0.80 g is what one 100 mL extraction gives (K = 4 gives 4/5 extracted). Two 50 mL portions do better.
Correct. Each 50 mL pass leaves 100/(100 + 4 x 50) = 1/3 in water. After two passes (1/3)^2 = 1/9 remains, so 8/9 or about 0.89 g is extracted.
Wrong. In a finite number of extractions, some solute always stays in the water. 100% is never reached.

p: The partition coefficient K = (concentration in organic) / (concentration in water). A bigger K means the solute prefers the organic layer.
The fraction left in water after one extraction is Vaq / (Vaq + K x Vorg). Repeat the extraction and multiply the fractions.

mem: Fraction left = Vaq / (Vaq + K x Vorg)
After n extractions, multiply the fraction n times
Extracted = 1 - fraction left

fm.f: Fraction left after one extraction = Vaq / (Vaq + K x Vorg), where Vaq = volume of water, K = partition coefficient, Vorg = volume of organic solvent used
fm.v: Vaq = 100 mL, K = 4, Vorg = 50 mL, two extractions, 1.0 g solute
fm.s: Fraction left = 100 / (100 + 4 x 50) = 100/300 = 1/3. Two passes: (1/3) x (1/3) = 1/9 left. Extracted = 1 - 1/9 = 8/9, about 0.89 g
fm.why: Each fresh portion removes the same fraction of whatever solute is still in water.
fm.nc: Only integers and simple fractions. 8/9 is just under 0.9.

x5C_011.trap: Stopping after one extraction (0.67 g) or using the one-big-extraction answer (0.80 g).
x5C_011.plain: Each rinse removes some fraction of the dirt left. Two rinses leave a fraction of a fraction, which is much smaller.

ox: Wrong. A column does not change any compound's boiling point. Boiling points are intrinsic properties.
Wrong. Condensing vapor into liquid is the condenser's job. The column's job is repeated re-vaporizing and condensing inside it.
Wrong. Nonvolatile impurities stay in the pot and never enter the vapor. The column enriches the volatile components rather than filtering.
Correct. The packed column lets vapor condense and re-vaporize many times. Each cycle (a theoretical plate) makes the vapor richer in the more volatile component.

p: A fractionating column is a tube packed with beads or metal that gives a large surface. Rising vapor condenses on it, then boils again, over and over.
Each round trip works like one extra simple distillation. The vapor gets richer in the lower-boiling component each time. Each round trip is called a theoretical plate.

mem: Column = many vaporization-condensation cycles
Each cycle = one theoretical plate
More plates = better separation
Column does not change boiling points
x5C_019.trap: Confusing the column with the condenser. The column repeats the equilibrium; the condenser just cools.
x5C_019.plain: It is like a relay race where each runner passes the baton only to the faster runner. After many passes the fastest team is left.

ox: Wrong. At a given temperature, vapor pressure is a property of the liquid. A vacuum lowers the outside pressure; it does not raise the vapor pressure.
Wrong. Decomposition from heat happens without oxygen too. Also, removing oxygen is not the main reason for using vacuum distillation.

Correct. A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the outside pressure. With less outside pressure, the liquid reaches that point at a lower temperature, below 250 °C, so it can be distilled without decomposing.
Wrong. The aim here is to lower the boiling temperature, not to change the gap between boiling points of different compounds.

p: Boiling happens when the liquid's vapor pressure (its tendency to escape as gas) equals the pressure around it. Normal boiling point is measured at 1 atm.
If you lower the outside pressure with a vacuum, the liquid boils at a lower temperature. This protects heat-sensitive compounds.

mem: Boiling: vapor pressure = external pressure
Lower pressure means lower boiling point
Use vacuum distillation for heat-sensitive or very high-boiling compounds
x5C_020.trap: Saying the vacuum changes the compound's vapor pressure. It changes the pressure it must match.
x5C_020.plain: Like water boiling at a lower temperature on a high mountain, where the air pressing down is weaker.

ox: Wrong. Ethanol boils at about 78 °C and water at 100 °C. They are different, so that is not the reason.
Correct. Ethanol and water form an azeotrope at about 95.6% ethanol. There the vapor and liquid have the same composition, so more boiling and condensing cannot enrich it further.
Wrong. Even an unlimited number of plates cannot go past the azeotrope. The limit comes from the mixture, not the column.
Wrong. Ethanol and water do not react at boiling. The limit is a vapor-liquid equilibrium effect.

p: An azeotrope is a mixture that boils at one fixed temperature and gives vapor with the same composition as the liquid. Because the vapor matches the liquid, distillation cannot change it.
Ethanol and water form such a mixture at about 95.6% ethanol. Fractional distillation can reach it but not pass it.

mem: Azeotrope: vapor composition = liquid composition
Ethanol-water azeotrope is about 95.6% ethanol
Azeotropes distill at one constant temperature
Better columns do not break azeotropes
x5C_023.trap: Blaming the column. The limit is the mixture's behavior.
x5C_023.plain: Like a mix of two paint colors that is so evenly blended that scooping it out always gives the same color.

ox: Wrong. 0.50 is the liquid composition. The vapor is richer in the more volatile liquid (A), so it must be above 0.50.

Wrong. 0.67 is 2/3, a 2:1 vapor ratio instead of the real 3:1. It also comes from 300/(300 + 150), where A keeps its full pure pressure but B is wrongly set to 150. Both A and B must be multiplied by 0.5, giving 150 and 50.
Correct. By Raoult's law, PA = 0.5 x 300 = 150 torr and PB = 0.5 x 100 = 50 torr. Total = 200 torr, so yA = 150/200 = 0.75.

Wrong. 0.90 is a 9:1 ratio. That happens if you square the 3:1 pressure ratio, or assume the vapor is almost all A because A is more volatile. Enrichment is only as big as the partial pressures say: 150 out of 200 is 0.75.

p: For an ideal mixture, each liquid's partial pressure equals its mole fraction in the liquid times its pure vapor pressure. Mole fraction means the part of the total moles that one substance makes up.
The vapor mole fraction is that liquid's partial pressure divided by total pressure. The more volatile liquid (higher P°) is enriched in vapor.

mem: Raoult: Pi = xi x P°i
Total P = sum of partial pressures
yi = Pi / Ptotal
Vapor is richer in the more volatile component

fm.f: PA = xA x P°A and yA = PA / Ptotal, where xA = mole fraction of A in liquid, P°A = pure vapor pressure of A, PA = partial pressure of A, yA = mole fraction of A in vapor
fm.v: xA = xB = 0.5, P°A = 300 torr, P°B = 100 torr
fm.why: An ideal liquid mixture obeys Raoult's law, so partial pressures set the vapor composition.
fm.nc: Halves and a 3:1 ratio, so 150:50 = 3:1 gives 3/4.

x5C_025.sc: With a 50:50 liquid, the vapor ratio equals the P° ratio. 300:100 = 3:1, so A is 3/4 of the vapor.
x5C_025.trap: Answering 0.50 because the liquid is 50:50. The vapor is enriched in the more volatile liquid.
x5C_025.plain: If two kids in a room are equally many, but one is much louder, the noise you hear is mostly from the louder one.

ox: Wrong. Flooding (too much liquid filling the column) disrupts flow and is unrelated to a clean temperature jump between two plateaus.
Wrong. An azeotrope distills at one constant temperature. It would not cause a sharp rise to a new level.
Wrong. A clean rise to a new steady level fits the second component's boiling point. Decomposition would not give a leveling-off plateau.
Correct. The steady temperature is the lower-boiling component's boiling point. When it is used up, the head temperature climbs toward the boiling point of the second liquid and levels off there.

p: The head temperature (at the thermometer) tells you which compound is distilling. While one pure liquid distills, the temperature stays flat at its boiling point.
When that liquid is nearly gone, the temperature rises until the next liquid starts to distill. That is a second flat plateau.

mem: Plateau = one component distilling at its boiling point
Sharp rise = the lower-boiling component is nearly gone
Change receiving flasks during the rise
Azeotrope = single constant temperature
x5C_026.trap: Calling a rise a problem. It is the normal transition between fractions.
x5C_026.plain: Like a pot of two foods cooking: one cooks off first, the temperature jumps, and then the second one starts.

ox: Wrong. Cooling first lets the dust be collected with the crystals, so the product would be contaminated.
Wrong. Insoluble particles do not dissolve, and extra solvent only lowers the final crystal yield.
Correct. Filtering the hot solution through fluted paper removes the insoluble dust while the product stays dissolved. Then cool the filtrate to make crystals.
Wrong. Charcoal adsorbs colored impurities onto its surface. It does not dissolve dust.

p: In recrystallization, you dissolve the solid in hot solvent, then cool it so pure crystals form. Dust that does not dissolve must be removed while the solution is hot.
Use gravity filtration with fluted paper. The product stays dissolved when hot, passes through, and crystallizes later in the filtrate.

mem: Insoluble impurities: hot gravity filtration
Colored impurities: activated charcoal, then filter hot
Soluble impurities stay in the cold solvent
Then cool slowly to form crystals
x5C_031.trap: Cooling first. Then the dust and crystals end up together.
x5C_031.plain: It is like pouring hot soup through a strainer to catch the bits before the soup cools.

ox: Wrong. 8 g wrongly counts 2 g lost. At 2 g per 100 mL, only 50 mL is present, so only 1 g stays dissolved.
Correct. At 0 °C, 50 mL holds 1 g (half of 2 g per 100 mL). So 10 - 1 = 9 g can crystallize. All 10 g dissolve hot because 50 mL holds 10 g at 80 °C.
Wrong. Some compound always stays dissolved in the cold solvent, so recovery cannot be the full 10 g.
Wrong. This halves the mass and ignores the solubility data given.

p: Solubility is how much solid dissolves in a given amount of solvent. It is higher when hot and lower when cold. When you cool the solution, the extra solid crystallizes.
The solid that stays dissolved in the cold solvent is lost. Maximum recovery = amount used minus what the cold solvent can hold.

mem: Hot solubility high, cold solubility low
Recovery = starting mass - mass dissolved at the cold temperature
Scale solubility to the actual volume used
Using too much solvent lowers yield

fm.f: Recovered = Mass used - (cold solubility x volume / 100 mL), where cold solubility = grams per 100 mL at 0 °C
fm.v: Mass used = 10 g, cold solubility = 2 g/100 mL, volume = 50 mL
fm.s: Dissolved cold = 2 x (50/100) = 1 g. Recovered = 10 - 1 = 9 g
fm.why: Only the solid above the cold solubility limit can crystallize.
fm.nc: 50 mL is half of 100 mL, so halve 2 g.

x5C_035.trap: Using the per-100 mL value without scaling to 50 mL.
x5C_035.plain: Warm water holds a lot of sugar. When it cools, extra sugar falls out as crystals, but a little stays dissolved.

ox: Wrong. Distillation separates liquids by volatility. It is not used to collect crystals from a solution.
Correct. Suction through a Buchner funnel quickly removes the mother liquor (leftover solution) and partly dries the crystals. It is the standard way to collect solid product.
Wrong. Gravity filtration is slower. It is used when the hot solution must be filtered or the liquid is wanted.
Wrong. Extraction moves solutes between liquids. It does not collect solid crystals.

p: After crystals form, you must separate them from the liquid they grew in, called the mother liquor. Vacuum filtration does this fast: suction pulls the liquid through a Buchner funnel.
Air pulled through the solid also dries it a bit. Wash with a little ice-cold solvent to rinse off impurities without dissolving much product.

mem: Solid is the product: vacuum filtration (Buchner funnel)
Liquid is the product or the solution is hot: gravity filtration
Wash crystals with a small amount of cold solvent
x5C_036.trap: Picking gravity filtration because it sounds like a basic filter. It is slow and used for hot filtration.
x5C_036.plain: Like using a vacuum-powered strainer to quickly pull water off pasta.

ox: Wrong. The lower spot (0.25) matches the starting alcohol, so it is not the ketone. Trap: assuming a new spot means the reaction is finished.
Correct. The ketone has no O-H, so it hydrogen bonds less with silica and travels farther (0.55). The spot still at 0.25 is leftover alcohol, so the reaction is not done.
Wrong. Ketones cannot donate hydrogen bonds, so they are less polar than alcohols. Trap: thinking C=O is more polar overall, when the O-H is what sticks to silica.
Wrong. The 0.25 spot is exactly where the starting alcohol ran, so starting material remains. Trap: ignoring the reference Rf.

concept.t: TLC on silica: polarity and Rf
p: Thin-layer chromatography (TLC) separates compounds on a plate coated with silica, which is polar. Rf (retention factor) = distance the spot moved / distance the solvent moved. Polar compounds stick to silica and move less (low Rf).
An alcohol has an O-H that hydrogen bonds to silica. A ketone has C=O but no O-H, so it sticks less and runs higher. A spot matching the starting material's Rf means some starting material is left.

mem: Silica is polar: more polar = lower Rf
Alcohol (O-H) is more polar than ketone, so alcohol has lower Rf
A spot at the starting material's Rf means the reaction is incomplete
x5C_042.sc: Compare each spot to the known starting material first. If one matches, the reaction is not done.
x5C_042.trap: Do not call the reaction complete while a spot still matches the starting material's Rf.
x5C_042.plain: Silica is like sticky tape. The alcohol has a sticky hand (O-H) that grabs the tape, so it barely moves. The ketone has no sticky hand and slides far.

ox: Wrong. Running the same conditions again just repeats the same match. Trap: confusing reproducibility with identity.
Wrong. Many different compounds absorb UV light, so this does not tell compounds apart. Trap: treating a shared property as proof of identity.
Wrong. Spot size reflects how much sample was applied, not what it is. Trap: reading amount as identity.
Correct. Two different compounds can match by chance in one solvent. A co-spot in a second, different eluent that still gives a single spot makes a coincidence very unlikely.

p: Rf depends on the compound and the solvent. Two different compounds can share an Rf in one solvent by chance, so one match is weak evidence.

A co-spot means spotting the unknown and the known sample on top of each other in one lane. If they are different, you usually see two spots or a stretched spot. Using a second, different solvent system tests them in a new way.

mem: Same Rf in one solvent is not proof of identity
Co-spot: one spot = likely same; two or elongated spot = different
Confirm with a second, different eluent
x5C_044.trap: Repeating the same test, or using UV or spot size, cannot rule out a coincidental match.
x5C_044.plain: Two kids might be the same height by chance. If they also match in shoe size and hair color, you believe they are twins.

ox: Wrong. In pure hexane Rf is 0.00, so the compound would stay stuck at the top of the column. Trap: picking the weakest solvent.
Wrong. Rf 0.95 means it travels with the solvent front and will not separate from impurities. Trap: thinking faster is better.
Correct. Mixing hexane and ethyl acetate lets you tune the Rf to about 0.3. That gives good separation and the compound still comes off the column.
Wrong. Water is not used with silica columns, and it would deactivate the silica. Trap: assuming the most polar solvent is best.

concept.t: Choosing a column eluent from TLC
p: The eluent is the solvent that carries compounds through the column. TLC is a quick test to pick it. An Rf near 0.2 to 0.4 usually works best for a column.
Hexane is nonpolar and ethyl acetate is more polar. Mixing them gives a middle polarity. More ethyl acetate raises Rf. Less lowers it.

mem: Aim for target Rf about 0.2 to 0.4
Rf 0 = stuck; Rf near 1 = no separation
On silica, more polar solvent raises Rf
x5C_049.trap: An extreme eluent fails: pure weak solvent gives Rf 0, pure strong solvent gives Rf near 1. The answer is a mixture.
x5C_049.plain: Too little push and the toy car never leaves the start. Too much and it zooms past everyone. You want a medium push.

ox: Wrong. At pH 2.5 the acid is mostly protonated (neutral), not ionized. Ionization happens at pH 7. Trap: reversing the direction of the pH change.
Correct. Below its pKa the acid is mostly neutral RCOOH. It is more hydrophobic and sticks to the C18 phase longer, so retention time increases.
Wrong. Ionization state changes polarity, and polarity drives reverse-phase retention. Trap: thinking only the solvent mix matters.
Wrong. C18 is a chain of carbon and hydrogen with no ionizable groups, so it never becomes charged. Trap: blaming the column.

p: In reverse-phase HPLC, the column (C18) is nonpolar and the mobile phase is polar. Nonpolar compounds stick longer and have longer retention times. Charged compounds are polar and come off early.
A carboxylic acid is neutral (RCOOH) when pH is below its pKa and charged (RCOO-) when pH is above. Lowering pH makes it neutral, so it is retained longer.

mem: Reverse phase: nonpolar column, polar mobile phase
Neutral = more retained; charged = elutes early
Acid is neutral when pH < pKa

fm.f: pH - pKa = n, so ratio [A-]/[HA] = 10^n, where A- = ionized acid, HA = neutral acid
fm.why: Henderson-Hasselbalch tells how much acid is neutral at a given pH.
fm.nc: Difference of 2 means 100:1, no log needed.

x5C_059.trap: Many students think low pH makes the acid charged. Acids are protonated and neutral at low pH.
x5C_059.plain: A charged molecule loves water and slides past the oily column. A neutral one is oily and clings to it.

ox: Correct. At pH 7.5 this protein is below its pI (9.0), so it is net positive. DEAE is also positive, so they repel and the protein flows through.
Wrong. At pH 7.5 it is well above its pI (4.5), so it is strongly negative and binds DEAE tightly. Trap: mixing up which proteins an anion exchanger binds.
Wrong. pH 7.5 is above its pI (6.5), so it is mildly negative and binds. Trap: thinking pI near 7 means no binding.
Wrong. Proteins with pI below 7.5 are negative and bind DEAE. Trap: forgetting to compare each pI to the buffer pH.

p: pI is the pH at which a protein has no net charge. Above its pI a protein is negative. Below its pI it is positive.
DEAE is an anion exchanger. Its resin is positively charged and holds negative proteins. Positive proteins are repelled and wash through.

mem: pH > pI: protein negative
pH < pI: protein positive
Anion exchanger (DEAE) binds negative proteins
x5C_068.sc: Compare pH 7.5 with each pI. A pI above 7.5 means it flows through.
x5C_068.trap: Keep the direction straight: DEAE binds negative proteins, so the positive (high pI) protein is the one that flows through.
x5C_068.plain: The column is a magnet with a plus side. Minus-charged proteins stick. Plus-charged proteins bounce off.

ox: Wrong. The pI 6.5 protein is less negative at pH 7.5, so it binds weakly and elutes with less salt, meaning earlier. Trap: ignoring charge strength.
Wrong. Different net charges mean different binding strengths, so they come off at different salt levels. Trap: assuming same column means same behavior.
Correct. At pH 7.5 it is 3 units above its pI, so it is more negative. It binds more tightly and needs the most salt to release.
Wrong. Salt ions compete for the charged sites and release bound proteins. Trap: forgetting how gradient elution works.

p: Bound proteins are released by raising salt (NaCl). Chloride ions compete with the protein for the positive resin sites.
The more negative a protein, the more strongly it binds. It needs more salt to be pushed off, so it elutes later.

mem: Tighter binding = more salt needed = elutes later
On an anion exchanger, lower pI means more negative at a given pH
Salt competes for resin charges
x5C_069.trap: Do not pick the protein that is closer to the buffer pH. The farther pI is below the pH, the stronger the binding.
x5C_069.plain: Strong magnets need a bigger pull to come off. The more negative protein is the stronger magnet.

ox: Correct. Same length means same mass and charge, so shape decides. Supercoiled DNA is compact and moves through the agarose pores fastest.
Wrong. The open, floppy circle is bulky and drags, so it is usually slowest. Trap: assuming a circle is compact.
Wrong. Linear DNA usually runs between the supercoiled and nicked forms. Trap: thinking a straight rod is fastest.
Wrong. Equal mass does not mean equal speed, since shape changes drag. Trap: thinking only size matters.

p: In gel electrophoresis, DNA is negative and moves toward the positive electrode. The gel is a mesh, so compact molecules slip through easier.
Supercoiled plasmid is twisted tight. Linear DNA is a stretched rod. Nicked circular DNA has a cut in one strand, so it relaxes into an open loop. Speed order: supercoiled, linear, nicked.

mem: Typical speed: supercoiled > linear > nicked
Same length means same charge-to-mass, so shape matters
DNA moves toward the anode (positive)
x5C_078.trap: With equal length, do not say all forms run together. Shape changes the speed.
x5C_078.plain: A tightly wound ball of yarn pushes through a bush easily. A big floppy loop catches on every branch.

ox: Wrong. This treats size as linear with distance. Halfway between 100 and 1000 is not 550 on a log scale. Trap: averaging the sizes.
Correct. 6 cm is halfway in log scale, so log size = 2.5 and size = 10^2.5, about 316, so about 300 bp.
Wrong. 200 bp is too small. Halfway in log space is about 316, not 200. Trap: picking a number nearer 100.
Wrong. 750 bp is too close to 1000. Trap: averaging with a linear scale and then leaning toward the big marker.

concept.t: Estimating fragment size from a gel
p: Over the useful range, distance moved is linear in log10(size), not in size. Smaller fragments move farther.
So find the midpoint of the logs. Log of 1000 is 3 and log of 100 is 2. Halfway between them is 2.5, which means 10^2.5, about 316.

mem: Distance is linear with log(size)
Smaller DNA runs farther
Halfway between 100 and 1000 in log space is about 316

fm.f: log(size) interpolated linearly with distance, where size = fragment length in bp
fm.v: 1000 bp = 4 cm (log 3); 100 bp = 8 cm (log 2); unknown at 6 cm
fm.s: 6 cm is halfway, so log size = (3 + 2)/2 = 2.5; size = 10^2.5 = 10^2 x 10^0.5, about 100 x 3 = 300 bp
fm.why: The problem says distance is linear in log(size).
fm.nc: 10^0.5 is the square root of 10, about 3.

x5C_079.sc: Halfway on distance means halfway on the log scale, so about 3 times the smaller size.
x5C_079.trap: Averaging 100 and 1000 gives 550. That ignores the log scale.
x5C_079.plain: Think of a ruler where each step multiplies the number by 10. The middle of the ruler is not the middle number.

ox: Wrong. At pH 8.8 it is only 2.3 units above its pI, so it is less negative and moves slower. Trap: thinking a pI nearer the pH moves farther.
Correct. pH 8.8 is farther above pI 5.0, so it carries more negative charge. With equal mass, it moves faster toward the anode.
Wrong. Native PAGE keeps proteins folded, so charge and shape both affect speed. Trap: mixing up native PAGE with SDS-PAGE.
Wrong. Both are negative at pH 8.8 and enter the gel, moving toward the anode. Trap: forgetting to compare pH with pI.

p: Native PAGE runs proteins without SDS, so they keep their folded shape and their own charge. Speed depends on net charge, size and shape.
A protein is negative when buffer pH is above its pI, and the farther above, the more negative. More negative proteins of equal size move faster toward the anode (positive electrode).

mem: Native PAGE: charge, size and shape matter
SDS-PAGE: mostly mass
Lower pI means more negative at a given pH
x5C_087.trap: Do not use the SDS-PAGE rule (mass only) for native PAGE.
x5C_087.plain: Two runners the same size, but one has a stronger motor. The one with more charge runs faster.

ox: Correct. Phosphate adds negative charge, so the pI drops and the spot shifts toward lower pI in the IEF dimension. The mass change is too small to see.
Wrong. A phosphate adds only about 80 Da, which is tiny compared with a typical protein. Trap: assuming any added group changes size noticeably.
Wrong. Adding a negative group lowers pI, not raises it. Trap: reversing the direction of the charge effect.
Wrong. IEF separates charge isoforms, including phosphoforms. Trap: thinking 2D gels only see big differences.

p: 2D gels separate proteins twice. First, isoelectric focusing (IEF) sorts by pI (the pH where net charge is zero). Second, SDS-PAGE sorts by mass.
A phosphate group is negatively charged, so it lowers the pI. It adds only about 80 Da, too small to see by mass. So phosphoforms appear as a row of spots at the same size but different pI.

mem: Dimension 1 = IEF (pI); dimension 2 = SDS-PAGE (mass)
Phosphate adds negative charge and lowers pI
Phosphoforms form a horizontal row of spots
x5C_090.trap: A small modification changes charge much more than mass. Look at the IEF dimension.
x5C_090.plain: Two kids weigh the same, but one wears a magnet backpack. A magnet test spots the difference but a scale cannot.

ox: Wrong. Glycine moves toward the anode only when pH is above its pI, so it is net negative. At pH 3 it is below the pI. Trap: mixing up anode and cathode.
Wrong. It would stay put only at pH 6.0, its pI. Trap: forgetting to compare pH with pI.
Wrong. Protons swap rapidly, so every molecule has the same average positive charge, and all move the same way. Trap: thinking some molecules are positive and some negative.
Correct. pH 3 is below the pI of 6.0, so glycine has a net positive charge and moves to the negative electrode, the cathode.

p: The pI is the pH where an amino acid has no net charge. When pH is below pI, there are extra protons, so the net charge is positive. When pH is above pI, it is negative.
In an electric field, positive molecules move to the cathode (negative electrode). Negative molecules move to the anode (positive electrode).

mem: pH < pI: net positive; moves to cathode
pH > pI: net negative; moves to anode
pH = pI: no net charge; does not move
x5C_091.mn: Cations go to the Cathode: both start with C, as in CAT-ion to CAT-hode.
x5C_091.trap: Always compare pH with pI first, then match opposite charges.
x5C_091.plain: Opposites attract. A plus-charged molecule runs to the minus pole.

ox: Wrong. Lysine is positive at pH 6.0 (below its pI of 9.7) and glycine is neutral. Trap: assuming all amino acids move the same way.
Correct. At pH 6.0, aspartate (pI 2.8) is above its pI so negative, going to the anode. Glycine (pI 6.0) is neutral and stays. Lysine (pI 9.7) is below its pI so positive, going to the cathode.
Wrong. This reverses the charges. Lysine is positive and goes to the cathode. Trap: mixing up which amino acid is acidic or basic.
Wrong. Only glycine has zero net charge at pH 6.0. Aspartate and lysine are still charged overall. Trap: thinking every zwitterion is neutral overall.

concept.t: pI and migration of several amino acids
p: Compare buffer pH with each pI. Above pI means negative (goes to the anode). Below pI means positive (goes to the cathode). Equal means neutral (stays).
Acidic amino acids like aspartate have low pI. Basic amino acids like lysine have high pI. Glycine is in the middle.

mem: Aspartate pI about 2.8 (acidic)
Glycine pI about 6.0 (neutral)
Lysine pI about 9.7 (basic)
pH > pI: negative; pH < pI: positive
x5C_092.trap: A zwitterion has both charges but may still have a net charge. Only pH = pI means net zero.
x5C_092.plain: Everyone gets a vote on which pole to run to. Acidic ones lean minus, basic ones lean plus, and glycine at its pI stands still.

ox: Wrong. Sucrose stays dissolved in solution during the run. Trap: inventing a physical problem with the gradient.
Wrong. Particles denser than the gradient keep sinking and do not reverse. Reversal and banding happen in isopycnic centrifugation. Trap: confusing the two methods.
Wrong. The time limit is to keep bands separated, not to protect proteins. Trap: assuming centrifugation always denatures.
Correct. If the run continued, every particle would reach the bottom and pile together, losing the separation. Stopping captures them as separate bands.

p: In rate-zonal centrifugation, a sample is layered on a sucrose gradient and spun. Particles sink at different speeds, based on size and shape. Bigger, denser particles sink faster.

The gradient is not dense enough to stop them. So the run must be stopped while the particles are still spread out. In isopycnic (equilibrium) centrifugation, particles stop where their density equals the gradient.

mem: Rate-zonal separates by sedimentation rate (size and shape)
Run must be stopped early
Isopycnic separates by density and runs to equilibrium
x5C_097.trap: Do not mix up rate-zonal (stop before the bottom) with isopycnic (run to equilibrium).
x5C_097.plain: A race. If you wait until everyone reaches the finish line, you cannot tell who was fastest. Take the photo mid-race.

ox: Wrong. Salting out is reversible and non-covalent. Trap: thinking precipitation means chemical bonding.
Correct. High salt ions hold many water molecules, leaving less water to dissolve the protein. Proteins then clump and precipitate, which is called salting out.
Wrong. Ammonium sulfate is not a reducing agent, and it usually keeps proteins folded. Trap: mixing it up with DTT or beta-mercaptoethanol.
Wrong. Salt does not change a protein's pI. Trap: confusing salting out with isoelectric precipitation.

p: Proteins stay dissolved because water molecules surround them. Add lots of salt like ammonium sulfate, and the ions grab the water. The protein loses its water coat.
Then proteins stick to each other and precipitate. Different proteins precipitate at different salt levels, so this step can separate them. It is gentle and reversible.

mem: Salting out: high salt reduces protein solubility
It is reversible and does not denature
Different proteins precipitate at different salt concentrations
x5C_098.trap: Do not call salting out denaturation or cross-linking. It is a reversible solubility effect.
x5C_098.plain: Salt is like greedy kids grabbing all the water balloons. The proteins, left without water, huddle together.

ox: Wrong. This divides 600 units by 100 and does not compare specific activities. Trap: using a made-up ratio instead of activity per mg.
Correct. Specific activity goes from 1000/200 = 5 units/mg to 600/10 = 60 units/mg. Fold purification = 60/5 = 12.
Wrong. 200/10 = 20 only counts the protein removed and ignores that activity was also lost. Trap: using the protein ratio alone.
Wrong. 600/1000 = 0.6 is the yield, the fraction of activity recovered. Trap: confusing yield with purification.

p: Specific activity = enzyme units per mg of total protein. It measures how pure the enzyme is. Purer samples have higher specific activity.
Fold purification = specific activity after / specific activity before. Yield = activity after / activity before, which tells how much enzyme was kept.

mem: Specific activity = units / mg protein
Fold purification = final SA / starting SA
Yield = final units / starting units

fm.f: Specific activity (SA) = total units / total mg protein; fold = SA after / SA before
fm.v: Before: 1000 units, 200 mg. After: 600 units, 10 mg
fm.why: Fold purification compares activity per mg of protein before and after.
fm.nc: All divisions work out to whole numbers.

x5C_100.trap: Using protein ratio (20) or yield (0.6) instead of the ratio of specific activities.
x5C_100.plain: If 5 of every 100 marbles in a bag are gold, then later 60 of every 100 are gold, the gold is 12 times more concentrated.

ox: Correct. Size-exclusion has low loading capacity, since the sample must be a small part of the column volume, and it dilutes the sample. So it follows steps that concentrate and clean up the protein.
Wrong. Gel filtration is gentle and does not denature proteins. Trap: confusing it with harsh methods.
Wrong. Salt removal is possible but is not why it is placed late. Trap: picking a true side fact that does not answer the question.
Wrong. Its capacity is relatively low, not highest. Trap: reversing the key feature.

p: Size-exclusion (gel filtration) separates proteins by size. Small proteins enter the beads and take a longer path. Large proteins go around and elute first.
It can only handle a small sample volume and it dilutes the sample. So it is used late, as a polishing step, after high-capacity steps like ion exchange or affinity.

mem: Gel filtration: large molecules elute first
Low capacity and dilutes sample, so used late
Early steps are high-capacity (salting out, ion exchange)
x5C_102.trap: The key feature is low capacity, not denaturation or high capacity.
x5C_102.plain: A tiny coffee filter works great for the last bit of cleaning, but you would not pour a whole bathtub through it.

ox: Wrong. SDS is a detergent that unfolds the protein, so it is no longer native. The trap is picking the sharpest separation without checking the 'keep native' condition.
Correct. Size-exclusion (gel filtration) separates by size using gentle buffer, so the protein stays folded. The contaminants differ in size, so they elute at different times.
Wrong. The contaminants stuck to the Ni column once, so they will stick again. Repeating the same step gives the same result. The trap is thinking 'more of the same' means more purity.
Wrong. Heat unfolds most proteins and makes them clump, including your target. The trap is forgetting that boiling is not gentle.

p: Chromatography separates a mixture by passing it through a column. In size-exclusion (gel filtration), the column is packed with porous beads. Small proteins enter the pores and take a long path. Large proteins skip the pores and come out first.
The buffer is gentle, so the protein keeps its folded, working (native) shape. This makes it a good polishing step after affinity purification.

mem: Gel filtration separates by size; large proteins elute first
It is native (non-denaturing)
SDS and boiling denature proteins
Repeating the same affinity step does not remove co-purifying contaminants
x5C_104.trap: Choosing a repeat of the same column or a denaturing method. The question says contaminants differ in size and the protein must stay native.
x5C_104.plain: Imagine a crowd walking through a room full of small tunnels. Little kids dive into the tunnels and take longer. Big adults walk around and exit first.

ox: Wrong. Making a salt only swaps a proton for an ammonium partner. It does not flip any stereocenter. The trap is imagining the reagent changes the acid's shape.
Wrong. The salts are not enantiomers. Enantiomers have identical boiling points, solubilities and melting points in an achiral setting, so they could not be separated this way.
Wrong. Both enantiomers react and both form salts. Nothing is destroyed. The trap is confusing resolution with kinetic resolution.

Correct. A pure (R)-amine with R-acid gives (R,R). With S-acid it gives (S,R). These are not mirror images, so they are diastereomers with different solubilities and can be separated by crystallization.

concept.t: Resolution with a chiral resolving agent
p: Enantiomers are mirror-image molecules. They have the same melting point, solubility and boiling point, so they are hard to separate. Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images. They do have different physical properties.
Adding one pure enantiomer of a chiral partner turns a pair of enantiomers into a pair of diastereomers. Then you can separate them, for example by crystallization.

mem: Enantiomers: identical physical properties (except rotation)
Diastereomers: different physical properties
Resolution = make diastereomeric salts, crystallize, then recover each enantiomer with acid or base
x5C_105.trap: Thinking the salts are enantiomers or that one enantiomer is destroyed. Both react, and the products become diastereomers.
x5C_105.plain: Two identical left and right gloves look the same to a table. If each is paired with a right-handed person's hand, the two pairs now fit differently, so you can sort them.

ox: Wrong. HCl removes the amine only. The carboxylic acid stays neutral in HCl and remains in the ether. The trap is forgetting there are two different impurities.
Wrong. Brine (saturated NaCl) pulls water out of the organic layer. It does not ionize the acid or the amine, so neither moves.
Wrong. Bicarbonate removes the carboxylic acid only. The amine stays neutral in base and remains in the ether.
Correct. HCl protonates the amine to an ammonium ion that dissolves in water. NaHCO3 deprotonates the carboxylic acid to a carboxylate that dissolves in water. The neutral product stays in ether.

p: Charged molecules dissolve in water. Neutral molecules dissolve in organic solvents such as ether. By changing pH, you can turn an impurity into its charged form and wash it into the water layer.
Acid protonates amines (R-NH3+). Base deprotonates carboxylic acids (R-COO-). The neutral product is unaffected.

mem: Amine impurity: wash with dilute acid (HCl)
Carboxylic acid impurity: wash with weak base (NaHCO3)
Neutral product stays in the organic layer
Brine only helps dry the organic layer
x5C_108.trap: Using only one wash. Each wash removes just one type of impurity, so two impurities need two washes.
x5C_108.plain: Think of a net that only catches fish wearing a red jacket. You put red jackets on the unwanted fish so the net pulls them out and leaves your fish.

ox: Wrong. At 60% your target has precipitated, so it is in the pellet. Keeping the supernatant throws the target away.
Correct. At 40% the proteins that precipitate earlier form a pellet, which you discard. The target stays dissolved. Raising to 60% makes the target precipitate, and you keep that pellet.
Wrong. The target does not precipitate until above 40%, so at 40% it is still dissolved in the supernatant.
Wrong. At 100% nearly every protein precipitates, so you get little enrichment.

p: Adding a lot of salt such as ammonium sulfate takes water away from proteins. They clump and fall out of solution. This is called salting out. Different proteins precipitate at different salt levels.
To purify, you use two cuts. The first cut removes proteins that precipitate earlier than your target. The second cut collects your target.

mem: Salting out: high salt removes water shell and proteins precipitate
Low cut: discard the pellet. High cut: keep the pellet
Target precipitates between the two cuts
x5C_110.trap: Keeping the wrong fraction. Throw away the first pellet, keep the second.
x5C_110.plain: It is like a sieve with two sizes. First you remove the big rocks, then you catch the pebbles and let the sand go through.
